solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Fuel made a mess of chimney

indicators.note: to make a mess of something is to jumble it, so the four letters of the clue's first word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Somebody's careless handling of fuel has dirtied the chimney.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made a mess of' shuffles FUEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A flue is the duct or passage inside a chimney that carries smoke away, so the two are used interchangeably.

clue.text: See 13 across
Objections over cigarette end

indicators.note: in a down clue 'over' tells us to turn the word for objections upside down, reading it from bottom to top

parts.note: buts are objections, as in 'no ifs or buts'

explanation.surface: Someone raises objections about a stubbed-out cigarette butt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns BUTS round.
explanation.definitionFit: The stub is the short remnant left when a cigarette has been smoked, a synonym for butt.

clue.text: Pointer about one of life's essentials

indicators.note: 'about' here means turned around or rearranged, telling us to scramble the letters of the dog's name Pointer

explanation.surface: A gundog, the Pointer, is presented as something people can't live without.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges POINTER; the dog breed looks like the definition but is pure fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Proteins are nutrients every living organism needs, so the phrase describes one of them loosely but fairly.

clue.text: Ill-disposed to clam up about new hospital department

indicators.note: 'about' means surrounding, so the shuffled letters go round the abbreviation for new
'up' in the sense of disturbed or in disarray signals that the letters of 'to clam' are mixed

parts.note: ENT is the ear, nose and throat department of a hospital

explanation.surface: A clam refusing to open up is cast as a sulky patient in a hospital ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' shuffles TO CLAM into MALCOT, and 'about' wraps that round N to give MALCONT. 'to' looks like a link but is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A malcontent is a discontented, rebellious person, someone ill-disposed towards authority; here the noun stands as an adjective.

clue.text: Sheltered from reality minor celebrity welcomes round journalist

indicators.note: to welcome is to take in, so the celebrity word contains the circular letter

parts.note: a C-lister is a celebrity of the third rank
O is round in shape
ED is the usual crossword abbreviation for an editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A sheltered minor celebrity receives a visiting journalist for an interview.
explanation.walkthrough: 'welcomes' puts O inside CLISTER, after its L, giving CLOISTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone cloistered lives a secluded life as in a monastery, protected from the harshness of the outside world.

clue.text: Insufficiently lit to mount long shot

parts.note: a dimly lit place is dark
a mount is a horse one rides

explanation.surface: Climbing on a horse in poor light is a risky business.
explanation.definitionFit: A dark horse is a little-known competitor who may surprise, an outsider in betting terms.

clue.text: Get away with singing nonsense

definitions.meaning: an order to go away quickly, a command to shoo
jazz singers improvise nonsense syllables in the style called ...

explanation.surface: Someone escapes while warbling gibberish.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a brusque dismissal like 'shoo!' and the improvised syllable singing of jazz vocalists such as Ella Fitzgerald.

clue.text: Anticipating flop Sting is source of surprise hit

indicators.note: to anticipate is to come before, so the word for sting precedes the word for flop

parts.note: to sting is to smart with pain
a show that bombs is a flop; a bomb is a failure

explanation.surface: The singer Sting appears to be bracing for a commercial failure that turns into a surprise hit record.
explanation.walkthrough: Sting the pop star is a red herring: here it is the verb meaning hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: A guided bomb strikes its target with precision, a surprise strike from the air, so it is the origin of an unexpected hit.

clue.text: Greeting beaten leader in retreat or one taking a stand perhaps

indicators.note: 'in' places the greeting and the leading letter inside the word for retreat

parts.note: to exit is to withdraw or retreat
hi is an informal greeting

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, here of 'beaten'

explanation.surface: A defeated leader is greeted as he retreats, or a trader at a show booth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beaten leader' looks like an ex-leader; it is just the B at the front of 'beaten'.
explanation.definitionFit: Exhibitors at a trade fair or show rent a stand to display their goods; 'perhaps' marks this as one example.

clue.text: Rogue knocking back half pint around noon

indicators.note: the reversed letters go around the abbreviation for midday
to knock back a drink is to down it, and here it signals turning the half-word backwards
half of a four-letter word is its first two letters

parts.note: M for meridian, or noon, as in a.m. and p.m.

explanation.surface: A rascal downs half a pint at around midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' takes PI from 'pint'; 'knocking back' reverses it to IP; 'around' wraps that round M.
explanation.definitionFit: An imp is a mischievous little devil, a scamp or rascal, which is what a rogue can loosely mean.

clue.text: Half of what's done in a lab is mischievous

indicators.note: only half of the eight-letter word is kept, the first four letters being dropped

parts.note: research is the investigative work carried out in a laboratory

explanation.surface: Lab work is described as having a playful, roguish side.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half of RESEARCH is kept, with RESE removed.
explanation.definitionFit: An arch look or remark is knowing and playfully roguish, so the adjective means slyly mischievous.

clue.text: Endless caterwaul of bagpipes could lead one to drink

indicators.note: without its ends: the first and last letters of the wailing word are removed

parts.note: skirl is the shrill wailing sound of bagpipes

explanation.surface: The relentless howl of bagpipes is enough to drive anyone to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing both ends of SKIRL leaves KIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Kir is a French aperitif of white wine with a dash of blackcurrant liqueur, cassis.

clue.text: Gawp over early pop star, humorist and husband or stay pro

indicators.note: 'over' signals reading the word for gawp backwards

parts.note: to gawp is to stare, much like taking a peek
Adam Faith was a British pop singer of the late 1950s and 1960s
a wit is a clever, funny person

explanation.surface: An onlooker stares at a list of old entertainers and a husband, urged to remain supportive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns PEEK round. Adam Faith was a British teen idol around 1960.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep faith with someone is to stay loyal to them, remaining on their side, which is staying pro.

clue.text: Butler's tool?

parts.note: a butler looks after a house and might be pictured spying through the opening by a door lock; the tool is a narrow saw

explanation.surface: A household servant's equipment is the subject of the question.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the nosy servant peering through keyholes; the answer is a real carpenter's saw for cutting holes.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow-bladed saw for cutting shaped holes, playfully linked to an eavesdropping domestic servant who stoops at doors.

clue.text: Common female society up against it in, say, Ireland

indicators.note: 'in' places society and the word for it inside the abbreviation for 'say'

parts.note: e.g., for example, is what 'say' means

indicators.note: up against means right next to, so the two pieces sit side by side

parts.note: 'it' is a coy word for sex or sex appeal
IRL is the international code for Ireland

explanation.surface: A vulgar woman from the Irish republic is pitted against polite society.
explanation.walkthrough: The Essex girl is a British stereotype of a brash, flashily dressed young woman from Essex, the county east of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The stereotype the phrase names is a vulgar, unrefined woman; common is British slang for lacking class.

clue.text: Organ keeping fresh left in attache case — that's unbelievable!

indicators.note: to keep is to hold, so the newspaper letters hold the word for fresh

parts.note: an organ is a newspaper; FT is the Financial Times
a fresh, breezy room is airy

indicators.note: 'in' places the letter for left inside the outer letters of 'attache'
the case of a word is its outside, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A newspaper's attache case seems to hold something too strange to be true.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' takes the shell of 'attache', A and E, and 'in' puts L between them for ALE.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairy tale is an incredible story, hence anything said that nobody could possibly believe.

clue.text: Savour wine event from which sparkling white is almost entirely banned

indicators.note: banned means kept out, so the letters are removed from the wine event

parts.note: a tasting is an event where wines are sampled

indicators.note: almost all of the wine's name is used, its first letter being dropped

parts.note: Asti is a sparkling white wine from Piedmont in Italy

explanation.surface: At a wine tasting, the cheap fizz is nearly banished to preserve the flavour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost entirely' takes STI from ASTI and 'banned' removes it from TASTING.
explanation.definitionFit: A tang is a strong distinctive taste or flavour, a synonym for savour as a noun.

clue.text: Medium and large primarily in gipsy-styled clothing

indicators.note: styled means fashioned anew, so these letters are rearranged into a new form
primarily means first of all, so the initial letters of Medium and large are taken

explanation.surface: Clothing sizes, medium and large, are on offer in a bohemian gipsy style.
explanation.walkthrough: M and L from 'primarily' join GIPSY and 'styled' mixes all seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A gymslip is a sleeveless tunic once worn by British schoolgirls, so it is an item of clothing.

clue.text: Good name for dog should involve nothing trendy

indicators.note: to involve is to include, so the dog's name takes in the zero

parts.note: Rover is a traditional name for a pet dog
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Choosing a hip name for a dog becomes a matter for advice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trendy' is a noun here, a trendy person.
explanation.definitionFit: A groover is a fashionable, with-it person, as is a trendy used as a noun.

clue.text: American city in ruins, abandoned and surrounded by water

indicators.note: abandoned means wild and unrestrained, signalling the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: LA is Los Angeles

explanation.surface: A deserted US city lies in ruins, cut off by floodwater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandoned' looks like part of the picture of desolation but is the anagram signal for LA and RUINS.
explanation.definitionFit: Insular means relating to an island, and an island is surrounded on all sides by sea.

clue.text: Chefs' sauce?

definitions.meaning: the ... family, Michel, Albert and Michel Jr, are famous French chefs working in Britain
a mix of flour and fat cooked together that thickens a sauce, hence the query

explanation.surface: A question about a chefs' sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: The query concedes that the cooked flour-and-butter mix is a sauce base rather than a sauce.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of a celebrated cooking family and the flour-and-butter base of many white sauces.

clue.text: Bake teeny crackers that might be a risk

indicators.note: crackers means crazy, so the letters of the two words go haywire

explanation.surface: Baking tiny biscuits is presented as a gamble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crackers' looks like biscuits in the baking picture; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A Yankee is a multiple bet on four selections combined in eleven wagers, so it is a gamble or risk.

clue.text: Perhaps Jacob knew Esau could hold the key

indicators.note: the two words 'knew Esau' hold the answer within them, across the join

explanation.surface: The Biblical twins Jacob and Esau, with Esau knowing the key to something.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacob, Esau's twin in Genesis, looks like a person; Jacob is also a breed of piebald sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacob is a British breed of spotted sheep with several horns, and a ewe is a female sheep.

clue.text: Idiot highlighted regularly

indicators.note: regularly means at fixed intervals, here every third letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A fool is highlighted again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: Every third letter of 'highlighted' (the 3rd, 6th and 9th) is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Git is British slang for a stupid or contemptible person, close to a fool or idiot.

clue.text: Housemistress's inclusive accommodation

indicators.note: inclusive means containing within, so the word for the housing is contained in the clue's first word

explanation.surface: A boarding-school housemistress has all-inclusive accommodation.
explanation.walkthrough: A semi is British slang for a semi-detached house, one of a pair joined by a shared wall.
explanation.definitionFit: A semi-detached house is a form of housing, one sense of accommodation.

clue.text: Amateur artist upended in crush in front of electronic painting

indicators.note: the crushing word comes before the letter for electronic
'in' places the turned letters inside the word for crush

parts.note: to quell a revolt is to crush it

indicators.note: upended means turned over, so the artist abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, an artist
E is the abbreviation for electronic, as in e-mail

explanation.surface: An amateur painter is knocked over in a crowd crush before an electronic artwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upended' turns RA into AR.
explanation.definitionFit: An aquarelle is a painting done in transparent watercolours, from French for watercolour.

clue.text: Learn by ear clarinet part

indicators.note: 'by ear' means as heard, so the word for learn is heard rather than seen

parts.note: to read a subject at university is to learn it

explanation.surface: Someone learns to play a clarinet part without sheet music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Learn by ear' looks like the idiom for playing without notation; 'by ear' signals the homophone.
explanation.definitionFit: The reed is the thin vibrating strip in a clarinet's mouthpiece that produces the sound.

clue.text: Lap up endless old films

indicators.note: endless means losing both ends, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: the flicks is an old-fashioned word for the cinema or its films

explanation.surface: Someone eagerly enjoys watching old movies again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lap up' suggests relishing the films, but it is the definition: a cat's tongue at work.
explanation.definitionFit: To lap up milk is to take it in with the tongue, just as a lick does.

clue.text: Wise wanting island to exhibit eagle?

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the comedian's first name loses a letter

parts.note: Ernie Wise was the straight man in the British comedy double act Morecambe and Wise

explanation.surface: A wise person, but not an islander, shows off an eagle.
explanation.walkthrough: Ernie Wise was half of Morecambe and Wise, the much-loved British TV comedy duo. 'Wise' looks like an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The erne is the white-tailed sea eagle; the query flags it as one kind among many.

clue.text: Dracula's not quite last to linger over neck

indicators.note: 'over' means turned over, so the word for linger is read backwards

parts.note: to lag is to linger or fall behind

indicators.note: the letter just before the end of the vampire's name, its second-last

explanation.surface: Dracula lingers over his victim's neck before biting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite last' takes Dracula's penultimate letter; 'over' reverses LAG. 'neck', which looks like the vampire's target, is the definition: brazen cheek.
explanation.definitionFit: Neck and gall both mean brazen cheek or nerve, as in 'What a nerve!'

clue.text: Passing Edinburgh's first Morrison's note odour

indicators.note: the opening letter of the Scottish capital's name is taken

parts.note: Van Morrison is a Northern Irish singer-songwriter; his first name is used
E is a musical note
a scent is a smell or odour

explanation.surface: A musician's passing visit to Edinburgh leaves a faint smell behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Van Morrison, singer of 'Brown Eyed Girl', supplies his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Evanescent means fading quickly from sight, as fleeting or transient as a passing moment.
